question: What made you want to pursue culinary arts as a career instead of just cooking as a hobby?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific pull toward professional cooking, not a vague love of food.

bullets: Point to a concrete moment or period that shifted cooking from hobby to goal
Show you understand professional kitchens differ from home cooking
Connect it to what you want from a career, not just a pastime
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd always cooked for my family, but the shift happened when I did a week's work experience in a local bistro and saw how fast and precise a real service is. I loved that pressure instead of being scared of it, and I realized I wanted the discipline of a kitchen, not just the freedom of my own. That week made me start reading about culinary school instead of just watching cooking videos for fun. I want a career where I'm getting better at a craft every single service, not just cooking when I feel like it.

commonMistakes: Saying only 'I love food' with nothing specific
Describing hobby cooking with no sense of what a career adds
Sounding like they haven't thought past enjoying cooking shows
followUps: What surprised you most about professional kitchens compared to cooking at home?

question: Why do you want to study culinary arts here specifically, rather than another school?
lookingFor: Specific research into the program's kitchens, faculty, or externship model, not generic praise.

bullets: Name a specific feature: an externship partner, a chef instructor, a specialty track
Tie it to a concrete gap in your own experience
Show you compared it to alternatives, not just applied to the nearest school
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I looked at three programs, and yours is the only one that puts students into working restaurant kitchens for a full externship in the second year instead of just a short placement. I've done home cooking and one summer job at a cafe, but I've never worked a real line, and that's exactly the gap I need filled. I also read that your pastry module is taught by someone who trained in classical French technique, which is the area I'm weakest in and most want to fix. It felt like the program built for someone at exactly my stage.

commonMistakes: Praising the school's reputation with no specifics
Confusing this program with a different school's offering
Giving reasons that would apply equally to any culinary school
followUps: What's a specific skill gap you're hoping this program closes?

question: Tell us about the first dish or cooking experience that made you fall in love with food.
lookingFor: A vivid, honest memory that reveals real early engagement with cooking, not a rehearsed line.

bullets: Describe a specific dish, person, or moment rather than a general love of eating
Explain what about it actually hooked you, technique, culture, or people
Show how that early spark grew into something more deliberate
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My grandmother used to let me stand on a stool and stir her tomato sauce for hours, and I remember being fascinated that raw tomatoes, garlic, and time could turn into something so different from where it started. I was maybe eight, and I started asking her why she added sugar or why she waited so long to add the basil. That curiosity about the why behind cooking, not just the eating, stuck with me and turned into me trying to recreate dishes from restaurants at home by my early teens.

commonMistakes: A vague 'I've always loved food' with no scene or detail
Focusing only on eating rather than cooking or making
A story that sounds copied from someone else's interview answer
followUps: Do you still cook that dish today? What have you changed about it?

question: What hands-on cooking or kitchen experience do you have, and what did you learn from it?
lookingFor: Real evidence of kitchen exposure, paid or unpaid, with honest reflection on what it taught them.

bullets: Describe the setting: home, part-time job, catering, work experience
Give one specific lesson or skill gained, not just 'I helped out'
Be honest about the level, this doesn't need to be professional to count
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I worked weekend shifts at a small catering company for about eight months, mostly on prep, chopping vegetables and portioning proteins before events. It taught me how much speed matters once you're doing the same cut two hundred times in a row, and how easily a whole prep list falls apart if you don't organize your station first. I also learned to take direction fast because the head chef didn't have time to repeat instructions during a rush. It's not glamorous work, but it's where I first understood what discipline in a kitchen actually looks like.

commonMistakes: Overstating experience that's really just home cooking
Listing tasks with no reflection on what was learned
Sounding embarrassed about low-level or unpaid experience
followUps: What was the hardest part of that job to get used to?

question: Which chefs, cookbooks, or food writers have influenced you, and why?
lookingFor: Evidence of genuine engagement beyond cooking shows, with a specific reason the influence matters.

bullets: Name something specific, a book, a chef, a technique, not just 'cooking shows'
Explain what idea or technique from it actually changed how they cook
Show breadth if possible, more than one influence or type of source
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've read Samin Nosrat's book on salt, fat, acid, and heat probably three times, because it was the first thing that explained why dishes work instead of just giving me a recipe to follow. It changed how I cook at home, I now taste and adjust instead of measuring blindly. I also follow a few chefs on video who break down knife technique step by step, which is how I taught myself proper cuts before I had any formal training. Between the two I've got a better sense of both the science and the craft side of cooking.

commonMistakes: Naming only a TV personality with no substance behind it
Claiming influences they clearly haven't engaged with deeply
Giving an answer with no connection to their own cooking
followUps: What's one idea from that book or chef that changed how you actually cook?

question: What does 'mise en place' mean, and why is it so central to professional cooking?
lookingFor: A correct, practical explanation of the concept and why it matters under service pressure.

bullets: Define it accurately: everything in its place, all prep and tools ready before cooking starts
Explain the practical reason it matters, speed and consistency during service
Ideally connect it to their own experience organizing a station or a home cook session
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Mise en place literally means everything in its place, and it's about having all your ingredients measured, chopped, and your tools laid out before you start cooking rather than scrambling mid recipe. In a professional kitchen during service there's no time to stop and dice an onion halfway through fifteen tickets, so if your station isn't fully prepped you fall behind immediately and it snowballs. Even cooking at home I've started doing this properly, laying everything out before I turn on the heat, and it completely changes how calm the actual cooking feels.

commonMistakes: Only translating the French phrase with no explanation of why it matters
Describing it as optional or just tidiness rather than essential to service
Confusing it with cleaning down after cooking
followUps: Tell us about a time poor preparation caused a problem for you while cooking.

question: Can you explain what the Maillard reaction is and why it matters in cooking?
lookingFor: A reasonably accurate grasp of the science and a real example of applying it deliberately.

bullets: Explain it's a chemical reaction between amino acids and sugars under heat, producing browning and flavor
Distinguish it from simple caramelization, which only involves sugar
Give a concrete cooking example where they use it deliberately
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The Maillard reaction is what happens when proteins and sugars in food react under high heat, usually above about 140 degrees Celsius, and it's what creates that deep brown crust and complex savory flavor on things like a seared steak or toasted bread. It's different from caramelization, which is really just sugar breaking down on its own without protein involved. I use it deliberately when I sear meat, I pat it completely dry first and don't crowd the pan, because moisture or overcrowding drops the temperature and you end up steaming the surface instead of browning it.

commonMistakes: Mixing up the Maillard reaction with caramelization
Giving the definition with no practical cooking application
Overstating confidence with an inaccurate explanation rather than admitting partial knowledge
followUps: Why does a wet or crowded pan stop this reaction from happening properly?

question: Can you name the classical mother sauces and give an example of a sauce derived from one of them?
lookingFor: Accurate recall of classical French sauce theory with at least one correct derivative example.

bullets: Name most or all of: béchamel, velouté, espagnole, hollandaise, tomato
Show understanding that these are bases other sauces build from
Give at least one correct derivative sauce as an example
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The classical mother sauces are béchamel, velouté, espagnole, hollandaise, and tomato sauce, and the idea is that most classical sauces are actually built from one of these five as a base. Béchamel, for example, is milk thickened with a roux, and if you add cheese to it you get a mornay sauce, which is what goes into a lot of gratins. I like the system because it means once you understand the base technique, you can improvise a whole family of sauces from it rather than memorizing each one separately.

commonMistakes: Naming fewer than three sauces or confusing them with derivative sauces
Listing the names with no example of a derivative
Describing them as unrelated recipes rather than a base system
followUps: Which of the five would you say is hardest to get right, and why?

question: What do you understand about safe food handling, for example around temperature and cross-contamination?
lookingFor: Basic but accurate food safety awareness, showing they take hygiene seriously before formal training.

bullets: Mention the danger zone concept, keeping food out of the temperature range bacteria grow fastest in
Explain cross-contamination and how to avoid it, like separate boards for raw meat
Show this is a habit they already practice, not just theory
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I know that bacteria grow fastest in what's called the danger zone, roughly between 5 and 60 degrees Celsius, so food shouldn't sit out at room temperature for long, and hot food needs to stay hot while cold food stays properly chilled. Cross-contamination is another big one, using the same board or knife for raw chicken and then vegetables without washing in between can spread bacteria even if everything looks fine. At home I already keep a separate board for raw meat and always wash my hands and tools between tasks, because I know that's non-negotiable in any real kitchen, not just something you do when you feel like it.

commonMistakes: Vague statements like 'I always keep things clean' with no real detail
Not understanding the temperature danger zone at all
Treating food safety as a minor concern rather than fundamental
followUps: What would you do if you noticed a colleague skipping a food safety step during service?

question: What basic knife cuts are you already familiar with, and why does consistency in cutting matter?
lookingFor: Some real familiarity with classic cuts and understanding of why uniform size affects cooking, not just presentation.

bullets: Name at least a couple of cuts correctly, like julienne, brunoise, or dice
Explain that consistent size affects even cooking, not just how it looks
Be honest about current skill level rather than overclaiming mastery
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm comfortable with a basic dice and I've practiced a julienne cut on carrots, though I know my knife work still isn't fast or perfectly even. What I understand is that consistency matters because if pieces are different sizes, they cook at different rates, so you end up with some pieces raw and others overdone in the same pan. I've been practicing at home specifically to build muscle memory and speed, because I know that's something instructors expect students to already be working on before they arrive.

commonMistakes: Claiming advanced knife skills with no real basis
Naming cuts without knowing why the technique matters functionally
Sounding defensive about being a beginner instead of honest and eager to learn
followUps: What knife skill are you most looking forward to improving in this program?

question: Tell us about a dish you ruined or a mistake you made while cooking. How did you handle it?
lookingFor: Honest ownership of a real failure and evidence of a concrete lesson, not a disguised success story.

bullets: Describe a genuine mistake with specific detail
Take ownership without deflecting blame onto ingredients or time pressure alone
Show what specifically changed in how they cook afterward
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I once tried to caramelize onions quickly on high heat because I was short on time before guests arrived, and they burned bitter instead of turning sweet, which threw off the whole dish I was building around them. I served it anyway rather than starting over, and everyone could taste it, which was more embarrassing than if I'd just been honest and started again. Since then I've learned to respect that some techniques genuinely can't be rushed, and now I plan my timing backward from the slowest step instead of the fastest one. It taught me that pride in trying to fix something quietly is worse than just admitting a dish needs to be redone.

commonMistakes: Choosing a 'failure' that's actually a humble brag
Blaming the recipe, ingredients, or equipment with no self-reflection
Describing the mistake with no clear lesson learned afterward
followUps: How would you handle the same situation if it happened during a timed exam or service?

question: What do you understand about how a professional kitchen team, or brigade, is organized, and why is that structure important?
lookingFor: Basic awareness of kitchen hierarchy and roles, and a mature view of why structure matters under pressure.

bullets: Show awareness of roles like head chef, sous chef, station chefs, and commis
Explain that the hierarchy exists for speed and clear communication during service, not just tradition
Reflect on where they'd expect to sit in that structure as a beginner
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: From what I understand the brigade system runs from the head chef down through sous chefs and station chefs to more junior cooks and commis, with each station responsible for a specific part of the menu, like sauces or grill. The structure matters because during a busy service there's no time for group discussion, someone needs to give a clear instruction and everyone needs to trust it and move, otherwise tickets pile up and the whole line falls apart. I know coming in I'd be starting near the bottom of that structure, and I actually want that, because I'd rather earn my way up by proving I'm reliable on the smaller tasks first.

commonMistakes: No real knowledge of kitchen roles beyond 'head chef'
Describing the hierarchy as unnecessary or overly strict without understanding its purpose
Assuming they'd start with more authority or responsibility than is realistic
followUps: How would you handle receiving a sharp correction from a station chef mid-service?

question: Culinary training involves a lot of direct, sometimes blunt feedback. How do you handle criticism of your cooking?
lookingFor: Genuine openness to harsh feedback with evidence they've actually experienced and used it before.

bullets: Acknowledge that kitchen feedback can be blunt and explain why that's actually useful
Give a specific real example of receiving and acting on criticism
Avoid sounding either overly thin-skinned or falsely unbothered
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A teacher at a cooking workshop once told me my risotto was gluey because I'd been stirring it too aggressively and adding stock too fast, and honestly it stung a little in the moment because I'd been proud of it. But I asked her to show me the right pace, and the next batch was completely different, so I'd rather have that direct correction than polite silence that leaves me making the same mistake. I know culinary training will involve a lot more of that, often faster and sharper than a classroom setting, and I'd genuinely rather be told exactly what's wrong than be left guessing.

commonMistakes: Claiming criticism never bothers them, which reads as unconvincing
Describing feedback they never actually acted on
Sounding defensive or like they'd argue back with an instructor
followUps: Tell us about a time feedback stung. How did you handle that feeling in the moment?

question: Walk us through how you'd balance the flavors in a dish that tastes flat.
lookingFor: Practical understanding of flavor elements, salt, acid, fat, sweetness, and how to diagnose and fix an imbalance.

bullets: Show a diagnostic approach, tasting and identifying which element is missing
Mention the main levers: salt, acid, fat, sweetness, heat, bitterness
Give a concrete example rather than only abstract theory
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: If a dish tastes flat I taste it slowly and ask myself what's missing, usually it's either not enough salt to bring the other flavors forward, or it needs acid to cut through richness and make everything feel brighter. A soup I made once tasted muddy and heavy until I added a small squeeze of lemon at the end, and it completely changed the dish without me touching the seasoning at all. I try to think of salt, acid, fat, and sometimes a little sweetness or heat as the main tools, and I adjust one at a time and taste again rather than guessing and dumping everything in at once.

commonMistakes: Jumping straight to 'add more salt' without a diagnostic process
Listing flavor elements with no real example of using them
Confusing seasoning adjustments with changing the whole recipe
followUps: What would you do differently if the dish was too rich rather than too flat?

question: Why does cooking with seasonal, locally sourced ingredients matter to a chef?
lookingFor: Understanding of flavor, cost, and sustainability reasons, not just a vague 'it's better for you' answer.

bullets: Mention flavor and quality, in-season produce genuinely tastes better and is cheaper
Touch on sustainability or supporting local producers
Show awareness this shapes real menu decisions, not just an abstract value
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Ingredients picked in season simply taste better, a tomato in August is a completely different thing from one flown in during winter, and it's usually cheaper too because it hasn't traveled far or been stored for months. There's also a sustainability side, shorter supply chains generally mean less waste and less environmental cost, and buying local supports the farmers actually growing the food. Practically I think it also makes you a better cook, because you're forced to build menus around what's genuinely good right now instead of relying on the same ingredients year round out of habit.

commonMistakes: A vague health claim with no real reasoning
Treating it as only an ethical stance with no practical or flavor argument
Showing no awareness that this affects actual menu planning
followUps: Can you think of a dish that only really works at a certain time of year?

question: How would you approach cooking for a guest with a serious food allergy?
lookingFor: A serious, safety-first attitude, not a casual 'I'd just leave it out' response.

bullets: Emphasize taking allergies seriously as a safety issue, not a preference
Mention checking for hidden allergens and cross-contact, not just the obvious ingredient
Show they'd communicate clearly rather than guessing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd treat it as a safety issue, not just a preference, because a serious allergy can be life threatening, not just uncomfortable. That means checking every component of the dish, including sauces and garnishes, for hidden traces of the allergen, and being careful about cross-contact, like using a separate pan or board rather than just wiping the one I already used. If I was ever unsure whether something was safe, I'd say so honestly and check rather than assuming, because guessing wrong is not a risk worth taking with someone's health.

commonMistakes: Treating allergies the same as a simple taste preference
Ignoring the risk of cross-contact, focusing only on the obvious ingredient
Sounding like they'd guess rather than confirm and check
followUps: What would you do if you weren't sure whether a sauce contained an allergen?

subtopic: Physical and mental demands of kitchen work
question: Kitchen work often means long hours on your feet, heat, and pressure during service. How do you know you're ready for that?
lookingFor: Realistic self-awareness about the physical demands, backed by some actual experience of sustained pressure.

bullets: Show they understand the demands are real, not romanticized from television
Reference actual experience of physical or high-pressure work, even outside a kitchen
Be honest rather than overpromising unlimited stamina
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I worked a summer job on my feet all day at a busy cafe counter, and I know that heat, noise, and constant motion for eight or more hours is genuinely tiring in a way that's different from anything academic. I don't think I'll find it easy, especially at first, but I know I handle pressure better when I'm moving and doing something with my hands rather than sitting and worrying, which is part of why kitchens appeal to me. I'd rather be honest that this will be hard than pretend I already know exactly what a full service feels like.

commonMistakes: Romanticizing kitchen work with no acknowledgment of the real physical toll
Claiming unlimited stamina with no grounding experience
Sounding unprepared for or dismissive of how demanding the work actually is
followUps: Tell us about a time you had to keep working accurately even when you were exhausted.

subtopic: Cuisine or chef that shaped their cooking
question: Is there a particular cuisine, culture, or chef that has shaped how you cook or think about food?
lookingFor: A specific, personal influence with evidence of real engagement, not surface-level name dropping.

bullets: Name a specific cuisine or influence with a personal connection
Describe a concrete technique or principle taken from it
Show respect for the cuisine's context rather than treating it as a trend
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My cooking has been shaped a lot by my family's Punjabi background, particularly how much patience goes into building a proper tadka or slow simmering a dal, techniques that taught me that flavor built in layers over time beats trying to season everything at the end. Outside my own background I've also studied a bit of Japanese knife work and the idea of respecting an ingredient's natural form rather than forcing it into something else. I try to bring that same patience and respect into whatever I cook, even something as simple as a weekday vegetable dish.

commonMistakes: Naming a cuisine with no specific technique or principle taken from it
Treating another culture's food as just a trendy aesthetic
Giving an answer with no personal connection to back it up
followUps: How would you bring that influence into a dish that isn't from that cuisine at all?

question: If you could put one dish on a menu that represents who you are as a cook, what would it be?
lookingFor: A specific, thought-through dish that reveals personality, technique awareness, and genuine creative reasoning.

bullets: Describe an actual dish with specific components, not a vague concept
Explain why it represents them personally, not just that it tastes good
Show some awareness of the technique or balance involved
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd put on a slow braised short rib with a bright pickled mustard seed relish on top, because I like dishes that pair something rich and patient with something sharp and quick, which is honestly how I approach most of my cooking. The braise takes hours and rewards patience, but the relish is something I can make in twenty minutes and it cuts right through the richness so the dish doesn't feel heavy. It represents me because I'm someone who likes long careful processes but also gets restless if a plate doesn't have some contrast or surprise on it.

commonMistakes: Describing a dish too vaguely to actually picture, like just 'pasta'
Choosing something purely because it sounds impressive with no personal reasoning
Ignoring balance or technique and focusing only on ingredients listed
followUps: What would you change about that dish if a guest said it was too rich?

question: Why do chefs need to think about food cost and portioning, not just taste and creativity?
lookingFor: Awareness that professional cooking is also a business, with some grasp of why cost control matters practically.

bullets: Explain that a restaurant has to be financially sustainable, not just serve great food
Mention that consistent portioning affects both cost and guest experience
Show they understand creativity has to work within real constraints, not despite them
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A dish can taste incredible and still lose the restaurant money if the ingredients are too expensive relative to what it's priced at, so part of a chef's job is designing dishes that are creative but still make financial sense to serve every day. Consistent portioning matters for the same reason, if one plate gets twice the expensive protein of another, that's both a cost problem and an unfair guest experience. I actually find that constraint interesting rather than limiting, because figuring out how to make an inexpensive ingredient taste incredible feels like a real creative challenge, not just a compromise.

commonMistakes: Treating cost and creativity as if they're unrelated to each other
No understanding that a restaurant is a business that needs to stay financially viable
Dismissing food cost as someone else's job, not the cook's concern
followUps: Can you think of an expensive ingredient you'd try to substitute without losing quality?

question: What does it mean to cook with a nose-to-tail or root-to-stem mindset, and why might that matter to you as a future chef?
lookingFor: Understanding of using whole ingredients to reduce waste, with a real example, not just a buzzword definition.

bullets: Define the concept correctly: using as much of an ingredient as possible rather than discarding parts
Give a concrete example, like using vegetable trim for stock or offal in a dish
Connect it to both sustainability and creativity or cost
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It means using as much of an ingredient as possible instead of throwing away parts people often consider scraps, like using carrot tops in a pesto or turning vegetable trimmings into a stock rather than the bin. I started doing this at home partly because it felt wasteful to throw away things that clearly still had flavor, and partly because it forced me to be more creative, a stock made from scraps I'd normally discard genuinely improved a soup I was making. As a future chef I think that mindset matters both because food waste is a real environmental problem in the industry, and because it often makes you a more resourceful cook.

commonMistakes: Defining the term without a concrete cooking example
Treating it as purely a marketing trend rather than a real technique
Ignoring the sustainability or cost angle entirely
followUps: What's an ingredient part you used to throw away that you now use in cooking?

question: How would you describe your approach to plating a dish?
lookingFor: A thoughtful, coherent philosophy that connects presentation to flavor and function, not just aesthetics for its own sake.

bullets: State a clear guiding principle, like restraint, height, or letting the main ingredient lead
Explain that plating should serve the eating experience, not just look nice
Show awareness of practical constraints like speed and consistency in a real kitchen
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I lean toward restraint, I'd rather have three elements that each have a clear purpose than ten things scattered across the plate for the sake of looking full. My rule for myself is that anything on the plate needs to be edible and add something to the bite, not just sit there as decoration. I also know that in a real kitchen, plating has to be something you can repeat consistently and quickly under pressure, so I try to design plates that look considered but aren't so fussy that they fall apart the moment you're plating fifteen of them in a row.

commonMistakes: Describing plating only in decorative terms with no connection to eating
Designing something impractical for repeated service without realizing it
Giving no personal point of view, just describing generic plating rules
followUps: What's a plating trend you don't like, and why?

question: How do you actively work on developing your palate as a cook?
lookingFor: Evidence of deliberate tasting practice, not just eating widely without reflection.

bullets: Describe a deliberate practice, tasting things side by side, tasting throughout cooking
Show curiosity about unfamiliar cuisines or ingredients, not just comfort foods
Connect it to actually improving their cooking, with a specific example
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I try to taste things side by side rather than in isolation, like comparing two olive oils or two vinegars back to back so I actually notice the difference instead of assuming they're interchangeable. I also make a point of trying cuisines I'm not familiar with when I get the chance, because it's easy to only trust flavors you already know well. Doing that helped me understand fish sauce properly, I used to think it just smelled strong, but tasting it deliberately in small amounts taught me how it works as a background savory note rather than a dominant flavor, and now I use small amounts of it in dishes that have nothing to do with the cuisine it came from.

commonMistakes: Claiming a broad palate with no actual practice described
Only mentioning eating out a lot with no deliberate tasting habit
Giving no specific example of a flavor they came to understand better
followUps: What's a flavor or ingredient you used to dislike but have learned to appreciate?

question: Where do you see your culinary career going after you finish this program?
lookingFor: A grounded, realistic direction that shows awareness of how careers actually progress in this industry.

bullets: Give a direction rather than an unrealistically specific title or timeline
Show awareness that early career means working up through kitchen roles
Connect the goal honestly to what draws them to cooking
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Long term I'd love to run my own small restaurant focused on the kind of honest, ingredient-led food I grew up eating, but I know that's realistically ten or more years away and starts with years of working stations under other chefs first. Right after graduating I want a position in a kitchen with a strong pastry and savory program so I can build broad technical skill before specializing in anything. I know the path isn't linear and I might end up somewhere I don't expect, but the constant is that I want to keep getting better at the craft itself, not just chase a title.

commonMistakes: An unrealistically precise plan with no sense of how kitchen careers actually progress
A goal disconnected from any real motivation or experience
Sounding like they'd skip paying dues in junior roles
followUps: What kind of kitchen would you want your first job after graduation to be in?

question: If you could only cook with three ingredients for the rest of the week, what would you choose, and what would you make with them?
lookingFor: Quick, genuine creative thinking under an odd constraint, revealing real cooking instinct rather than a rehearsed answer.

bullets: Choose ingredients that are versatile together, not just personal favorites with no logic
Suggest at least one or two concrete dishes possible from the combination
Show they're thinking on their feet rather than freezing at an odd question
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd pick eggs, onions, and good olive oil, because between those three you can genuinely build a huge range of things, a simple caramelized onion frittata, a Spanish style tortilla, or even just onions confit slowly in the oil to spoon over something else later in the week. I like that none of the three get boring on their own, the technique changes each time even if the ingredients don't. It's the kind of question that would've thrown me a year ago, but honestly thinking in constraints like this is part of what got me excited about cooking as a discipline rather than just following recipes.

commonMistakes: Freezing up or refusing to commit to an answer
Choosing ingredients with no real logic for how they'd combine
Naming ingredients but giving no actual dish idea
followUps: What's the first thing you'd get tired of, and how would you keep it interesting by day five?
